The official sample questions reveal a consistent grading philosophy. When two answers both "could work," the correct one almost always follows one of these principles:
Deterministic > probabilistic when compliance is mandatory.
Business-critical ordering (verify identity before refund) → programmatic hooks/gates, not prompt text or few-shot examples. Prompts have a non-zero failure rate.
Fix the root cause with the simplest proportionate change.
first, before few-shot examples, routing layers, or classifiers. "Over-engineered" is a recurring wrong-answer trap.
Self-reported confidence and sentiment are unreliable proxies.
Escalation should be driven by explicit criteria + few-shot examples, not confidence thresholds or sentiment analysis.
Match the API to latency tolerance.
Batch API (50% cheaper, up to 24h, no SLA) for overnight/weekly jobs; synchronous API for anything blocking.
Large multi-file reviews → per-file passes + a separate cross-file integration pass. Bigger context windows do NOT fix attention quality.
A fresh Claude instance without the generator's reasoning context catches more issues.
Nullable/optional fields where data may be absent; enums with "unclear"/"other"+detail; retries can't recover information that isn't in the source.
errorCategory, isRetryable, what was attempted, partial results. Generic failures, silent suppression, and whole-workflow termination are all anti-patterns.
Context must be passed explicitly in prompts; coordinator routes all communication (hub-and-spoke).
Claim–source mappings, publication dates, conflict annotation with attribution — never silently pick one value.
